title: Piano Concerto No. 1 in E minor
hook: A twenty-year-old’s farewell to Warsaw, with a slow movement he called a moonlit reverie.

painting.title: View of Morysinek
painting.pairingNote: Still water, a white villa and a rainbow after rain in a park on the edge of Warsaw, painted a few years after Chopin left the city for good; the gentle Polish light of the Romance.

facts: Chopin wrote it in Warsaw in 1830, when he was twenty. It was actually the second of his two piano concertos. It is called No. 1 only because it was published first.

He played it on 11 October 1830 at the National Theatre in Warsaw, in one of his farewell concerts before going abroad; a local paper counted about 700 listeners. Three weeks later he left Poland, and he never returned. Before the year was out, the November Uprising against Russian rule had begun.

It is a young pianist’s concerto, written for himself to play. The orchestra mostly frames and supports the piano, and the piano does nearly all the talking: long, ornamented melodies like an opera singer’s, and sparkling runs.

Chopin told his friend Tytus Woyciechowski that the slow movement was “a kind of reverie in the moonlight on a beautiful spring evening”. The finale borrows the rhythm of the krakowiak, a lively dance from Kraków.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a long, proud and songful Allegro (I), a moonlit romance (II), a Polish dance (III).

movements.heading: Allegro maestoso
movements.summary: The orchestra plays alone for almost four minutes, setting out the themes. Then the piano bursts in and takes over: it sings the same tunes with long, decorated lines and links them with glittering runs. The movement is long and in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], but it feels like a series of songs for the piano.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, proud
mainIdeas.description: a firm, stately tune in E minor, first played loud by the whole orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, longing
mainIdeas.description: a soft, singing melody in the minor, first on the strings.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 3, warm
mainIdeas.description: a gentle, rocking melody in E major, the brightest moment of the movement.

stops.hear: The orchestra alone, loud and stately; a firm tune in a proud, marching three-beat rhythm
The strings play a soft, longing melody
The piano crashes in with loud chords and octaves, then plays the proud tune itself
The piano alone sings a soft, sad melody, slowly, with delicate decorations
Brighter and calmer; a tender, rocking tune in the major
stops.happening: Theme 3, in E major. Not the key a listener of the time would have expected

stops.hear: Glittering runs and fast passagework in the piano, getting more and more brilliant
stops.happening: The piano’s display at the end of the [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: The full orchestra breaks in loudly, then the music grows restless and darker
The proud first tune returns
The rocking, tender tune again, now in a different key

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: Fast, stormy runs in E minor and a few loud chords from the orchestra

notice: Listen to how the piano decorates a slow melody. It adds trills, turns and little rushes of notes, like a singer ornamenting an aria.
The orchestra hardly ever plays while the piano sings. It waits, accompanies softly, and comes in loud only between the piano’s sections.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Argerich was 26. Three years earlier, in 1965, she had won the International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw, the city where this concerto was first heard. Her first movement lasts 19 minutes; Zimerman, in the alternative recording, takes more than 23.

movements.heading: Romance. Larghetto
movements.summary: A slow, dreamy song for the piano over [[muted|muted]] strings, close to the piano [[nocturne|nocturne]]s for which Chopin became famous. It is the “moonlit reverie” of his letter: calm, tender, a little sad. A restless passage in the middle passes, and the melody returns, more decorated than before.

mainIdeas.name: The romance
mainIdeas.description: a slow, singing melody in E major, richly decorated by the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: quicker, rustling figures in the piano, more troubled.

stops.hear: Soft, veiled strings play a short, hushed introduction
The piano enters with a slow, singing melody, decorated with trills and little runs
stops.happening: The main melody, in E major

stops.hear: The melody climbs and brightens, moving to a new key
stops.happening: A second idea, in a brighter key

stops.hear: More restless; the piano’s line breaks into quick, rustling figures over a darker harmony
The slow melody returns, now even more ornamented
High, delicate runs and slow trills in the piano, almost weightless

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The piano fades out in soft, high notes, and the strings close quietly

notice: The strings are muted throughout. Listen to their veiled, soft sound. It leaves the piano as the only clear voice.
Compare the melody at ≈ 0:45 with its return at ≈ 6:15. The tune is the same; the decoration is new.

movements.heading: Rondo. Vivace
movements.summary: A bright, dancing [[rondo|rondo]] in E major. The main tune bounces, with accents that land off the beat, the stamping rhythm of the [[krakowiak|krakowiak]], a dance from Kraków. The piano races through glittering runs and ends the concerto in a blaze.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo tune
mainIdeas.description: a quick, playful melody in E major, with little accents on the weak beats.

mainIdeas.name: The octave tune
mainIdeas.description: a second tune with both hands playing the same notes, and a heavy, stamping rhythm.

stops.hear: A short orchestral introduction with a quick, dancing figure
The piano plays a playful, bouncing tune; the accents fall off the beat
stops.happening: The rondo theme, in E major, in the rhythm of the [[krakowiak|krakowiak]]

stops.hear: Sparkling runs high on the piano
Both hands play the same notes, octaves apart, in a heavy, stamping rhythm with sharp accents
stops.happening: The second tune, in [[unison|unison]], with strong [[syncopation|syncopation]]

stops.hear: The playful tune returns
A new episode, in a different key, with more runs and dialogues with the orchestra
The playful tune once more
The stamping octave tune returns, now in the home key
Faster and more brilliant; the piano dashes up and down the keyboard

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A few bright chords for the orchestra

notice: Tap along with the rondo tune. You will feel a kick on the second half of the beat, not the first. That off-beat kick is the krakowiak.

threads.title: The piano as a singer
threads.body: Chopin’s piano melodies are decorated the way an opera singer decorates an aria: trills, turns and long, flowing runs.

threads.title: Goodbye to Warsaw
threads.body: It was written and first played in Warsaw, weeks before Chopin left Poland forever.

threads.title: Polish dance
threads.body: The finale’s krakowiak is one of the Polish dance rhythms that run through Chopin’s music, with his mazurkas and polonaises.

threads.title: Major and minor
threads.body: The first movement keeps turning from E minor to E major. The last two movements stay in the major, and the concerto ends in bright E major.
